sources.title: Tempo docs: Consensus and finality (Simplex BFT)
sources.notes: Simplex BFT by Commonware; blocks about every 600 ms (500 ms builder loop plus latency); deterministic finality; permissioned validator set.

sources.title: Tempo docs: Fees
sources.notes: No native token; fees in USD TIP-20 stablecoins via Fee AMM; bounded dynamic base fee (T7); 50,000-gas transfer cap about 0.0006 USD, quiet floor about 0.00003 USD; fees accrue to the proposing validator.

sources.title: Tempo Session Intent for HTTP Payment Authentication (draft-tempo-session-00)
sources.notes: Actions open, topUp, voucher, close; EIP-712 vouchers; 15-minute forced close grace period; sessionProtocol v1 and v2; session problem types.

sources.title: Tempo docs: TIP-20 specification and overview
sources.notes: decimals() always returns 6; 32-byte transfer memos; TIP-403 policy registry; T6 receive policies redirect blocked transfers to ReceivePolicyGuard. Overview at https://tempo.xyz/developers/docs/protocol/tip20.

sources.title: x402 Protocol Specification v2
sources.notes: Version history v2.0 dated 2025-12-9; merged via PR #705 on 2025-12-11.

terms.plain: In x402, a facilitator is a server that checks a client's signed payment and then broadcasts it to the network on behalf of the resource server. It exposes `POST /verify`, `POST /settle` and `GET /supported`, and it usually pays the gas. The x402 docs say it does not hold funds or act as a custodian, and a resource server can also verify and settle on its own.
terms.ste: In x402, a facilitator is a server that examines a signed payment and sends the payment to the network. The facilitator does not keep the funds of the client.

terms.plain: The terms a resource server will accept for one paid resource in x402. Each entry of the `accepts` array is a `PaymentRequirements` object with `scheme`, `network`, `amount`, `asset`, `payTo` and `maxTimeoutSeconds`, plus an optional `extra` object. In V2 the server sends the full `PaymentRequired` object, base64 encoded, in the `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header of a 402 response.
terms.ste: Payment requirements tell the client the price, the token, the network and the recipient of a payment. The server sends them in a 402 response.

terms.plain: The signed payment a client sends back after it picks one of the offered payment requirements. A V2 `PaymentPayload` holds `x402Version`, the chosen requirements in `accepted`, and a scheme-specific `payload` with the signature. Over HTTP it travels base64 encoded in the `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header (V1 used `X-PAYMENT`).
terms.ste: The payment payload contains the signed payment of the client. The client sends the payload in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header with the second request.

terms.plain: In x402, a scheme is a named rule set for how money moves, such as `exact`, `upto`, `batch-settlement` or `auth-capture`. The `scheme` field in each payment requirement picks one, and a separate per-network document says how that scheme works on EVM, Solana, Lightning or another network. Schemes keep the core protocol independent of any single chain.
terms.ste: In x402, a scheme is a set of rules for the transfer of money. Each scheme has one specification for each supported network.

terms.plain: The default x402 scheme: the client pays one fixed amount that the server names in advance. On EVM networks the client usually signs an EIP-3009 `TransferWithAuthorization` message, and Permit2 and ERC-7710 delegations are alternative methods. The facilitator submits the transfer, so the client does not need gas.
terms.ste: The exact scheme transfers one fixed amount for one request. The server sets the amount before the client signs the payment.

terms.plain: An x402 scheme for metered work where the final price is not known in advance. The client signs a Permit2 authorization for a ceiling amount, and at settlement the server charges the actual amount, which must not exceed that ceiling. A zero charge needs no on-chain transaction.
terms.ste: The upto scheme lets the server charge an amount up to a maximum. The client signs the maximum, and the server charges the actual cost after the work.

terms.plain: An x402 scheme that collects many small payments and settles them together. On EVM the client deposits into a payment channel, then sends a signed cumulative voucher with each request, and the server claims and settles many vouchers in one transfer. A separate `cloudflare:402` variant is credit backed: the client signs requests with RFC 9421 and Cloudflare bills that identity later.
terms.ste: Batch settlement collects many small payments and settles them in one transfer. On EVM networks, it uses a payment channel and signed vouchers.

terms.plain: An x402 scheme that copies the card pattern of authorize first, capture later. The client authorizes a hold, the server runs the work, then captures up to the held amount or voids the hold, and refunds stay possible until `refundDeadline`. On EVM the default contract is `AuthCaptureEscrow` from Base commerce-payments.
terms.ste: Auth-capture is an x402 scheme that holds funds first and captures the funds later. The server can capture, void or refund the payment.

terms.plain: The x402 V2 setting that fixes the order of verify, resource execution and settlement. `authorization` (the default) verifies, runs the resource, then settles. `upfront` settles before the resource runs, and `escrow` settles a deposit first and a final charge after. Servers declare a non-default flow in `extra.paymentFlow`.
terms.ste: The payment flow sets the order of verification, work and settlement. The default flow is authorization.

terms.plain: A discovery extension for x402. A resource server describes its paid endpoint (HTTP inputs and outputs, or an MCP tool) in the `bazaar` extension, and a facilitator lists those endpoints at `GET /discovery/resources`. Agents can then search a catalog of paid services before they call one.
terms.ste: Bazaar is an x402 extension for the discovery of paid services. A facilitator shows a list of the services that use this extension.

terms.plain: The number that identifies an agent in an ERC-8004 Identity Registry. It is the ERC-721 `tokenId` of the agent's identity token and is assigned in sequence when someone calls `register`. A globally unique reference pairs it with `agentRegistry`, a string of the form `{namespace}:{chainId}:{identityRegistry}`, such as `eip155:1:` plus the registry address.
terms.ste: The agentId is the number of an agent in the ERC-8004 Identity Registry. The registry gives the next number to each new agent.

terms.plain: The URI stored on-chain for an ERC-8004 agent that points to its registration file. The spec names `ipfs://`, `https://` and base64 `data:` URIs, and the owner or an approved operator can change it with `setAgentURI`. An `https://` file can change without any on-chain event, so only content-addressed URIs pin the content.
terms.ste: The agentURI is the address of the registration file of an agent. The owner of the agent can change the agentURI at any time.

terms.plain: A reserved metadata key in the ERC-8004 Identity Registry that holds the address where the agent receives payments. It defaults to the owner at registration and cannot be written through `setMetadata`. To change it, the owner calls `setAgentWallet` with a signature from the new wallet: an EIP-712 signature for an ordinary account or an ERC-1271 check for a contract wallet.
terms.ste: The agentWallet is the address that receives payments for an agent. A change to this address needs a signature from the new wallet.

terms.plain: The JSON document an ERC-8004 `agentURI` resolves to. It carries `type`, `name`, `description`, `image`, a `services` list of endpoints (for example A2A, MCP, web or DID), `x402Support`, `active`, a `registrations` list that binds the file to on-chain identities, and optional `supportedTrust` values. The spec publishes an example structure but no JSON Schema.
terms.ste: The registration file describes an agent and its service endpoints. The file also contains the on-chain identities of the agent.

terms.plain: An optional off-chain JSON document that adds detail to one ERC-8004 feedback entry. It repeats `agentRegistry`, `agentId`, `clientAddress`, `createdAt`, `value` and `valueDecimals`, and can add MCP, A2A or OASF context and a `proofOfPayment` object with a transaction hash. The on-chain `giveFeedback` call records its URI and, unless the URI is content addressed, a keccak256 `feedbackHash`.
terms.ste: A feedback file gives more data about one feedback entry. The file is off-chain, and a hash on the chain can protect its content.

terms.plain: The ERC-8004 contract where any address except the agent's owner and operators can record feedback about an agent. Each entry stores a signed `value` with `valueDecimals` and two optional tags, and it can be revoked by its author or answered with `appendResponse`. `getSummary` averages entries only for a list of client addresses that the caller supplies, which is the spec's defense against fake reviewers.
terms.ste: The Reputation Registry keeps feedback about agents. The owner of an agent cannot give feedback to that agent.

terms.plain: A call to the ERC-8004 Validation Registry in which an agent's owner asks a named validator to check a piece of work. The request carries a `requestURI` and a `requestHash`, and only that validator can answer with `validationResponse` and a score from 0 to 100. The Validation Registry is specified, but the contracts README lists no official deployment.
terms.ste: A validation request asks one validator to check the work of an agent. The validator gives a score from 0 to 100.

terms.plain: The Ethereum standard for non-fungible tokens, where each `tokenId` is unique and has one owner. ERC-8004 makes every agent identity an ERC-721 token, so an identity can be transferred and approved with ordinary NFT tools. ERC-721 status is Final.
terms.ste: ERC-721 is the Ethereum standard for unique tokens. In ERC-8004, each agent identity is one ERC-721 token.

terms.plain: A Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard contract keeps its state at a fixed address while the logic contract behind it can be replaced. In UUPS the upgrade function lives in the logic contract, so whoever passes `_authorizeUpgrade` can change the code. The deployed ERC-8004 registries are UUPS proxies with upgrade rights restricted to one owner address.
terms.ste: A UUPS proxy is a contract that keeps its address and data when its code changes. The owner of the proxy can replace the code.

terms.plain: A Chain Agnostic Improvement Proposal that names a blockchain with a `namespace:reference` string, such as `eip155:8453` for Base or a `solana:` genesis hash. x402 V2 uses CAIP-2 strings in its `network` field, where V1 used plain names such as `base-sepolia`. ERC-8004 builds its `agentRegistry` reference on the same pattern.
terms.ste: CAIP-2 is a standard text format for the identifier of a blockchain. x402 uses this format in the network field.

terms.plain: A Chain Agnostic Improvement Proposal that names an account by adding an address to a CAIP-2 chain id, for example `eip155:1:` followed by the address. The ERC-8004 feedback file example writes `clientAddress` in this form. It lets one string say both which chain and which account.
terms.ste: CAIP-10 is a standard text format for an account on a blockchain. The format adds the account address to a CAIP-2 chain identifier.

terms.plain: A chain-agnostic way for a wallet to prove it controls an account by signing a structured message, defined in CAIP-122. x402 has a `sign-in-with-x` extension: the server sends `domain`, `uri`, `nonce`, `issuedAt` and related fields, and the client returns a signed `SIGN-IN-WITH-X` header. It proves who the payer is, which lets a server recognize a returning client.
terms.ste: Sign-In-With-X lets a wallet prove control of an account with a signed message. x402 uses it in an optional extension.

terms.plain: The Ethereum standard for hashing and signing typed, structured data instead of opaque bytes, so a wallet can show the user what they sign. A domain separator (name, version, chain id, contract) binds the signature to one app and chain. x402 uses EIP-712 for every EVM payment signature, and ERC-8004 uses it for `setAgentWallet`.
terms.ste: EIP-712 is the Ethereum standard for signatures on typed data. The signature is valid only for one domain and one chain.

terms.plain: An Ethereum token standard, still in Draft, that lets a holder sign an off-chain authorization so that someone else submits the transfer and pays the gas. The signed message carries `from`, `to`, `value`, `validAfter`, `validBefore` and a random 32-byte `nonce`. It is the default method of the x402 `exact` scheme on EVM, and USDC implements it.
terms.ste: EIP-3009 lets a token holder sign a transfer that another party sends to the chain. Each authorization has a time window and a nonce.

terms.plain: The Ethereum standard for checking a signature when the signer is a smart contract wallet rather than a key. The verifier calls `isValidSignature` on the wallet contract and expects the magic value `0x1626ba7e`. ERC-8004 uses it when a contract wallet becomes an `agentWallet`, and the x402 Sign-In-With-X extension uses it to verify smart wallet signatures.
terms.ste: ERC-1271 is the Ethereum standard for the check of a signature from a smart contract wallet. The wallet contract tells the verifier if the signature is valid.

terms.plain: A Uniswap contract that adds signature-based approvals and transfers to any ERC-20 token, including tokens without EIP-3009. The holder approves Permit2 once, then signs transfers that can carry a witness with extra data. x402 uses Permit2 as an alternative `exact` method and as the only method of `upto` on EVM, through proxies at fixed addresses.
terms.ste: Permit2 is a Uniswap contract that lets a token holder sign a transfer for any ERC-20 token. The holder must approve Permit2 one time first.

terms.plain: The HTTP status code 402 Payment Required. RFC 9110 still lists it as reserved for future use, so each protocol that uses it defines its own meaning. x402 answers with 402 and a `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header, and MPP answers with 402 and a `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` challenge.
terms.ste: HTTP 402 is the status code for Payment Required. x402 and MPP use this code to tell a client that a resource needs a payment.

terms.plain: The standard HTTP response header that tells a client how to authenticate. MPP defines a new authentication scheme called `Payment`, so a 402 response carries one or more `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` challenges with `id`, `realm`, `method`, `intent` and `request` parameters. On 2026-10-11 the `Payment` scheme was requested in an Internet-Draft but not yet in the IANA registry.
terms.ste: WWW-Authenticate is the HTTP header that tells the client how to authenticate. In MPP, this header contains the payment challenge.

terms.plain: The standard HTTP request header that carries credentials. In MPP the client retries the request with `Authorization: Payment` followed by a base64url credential, or with `Payment-Authorization` when the challenge asks for that header so the normal `Authorization` header stays free for other logins. A request with more than one Payment credential should be rejected.
terms.ste: The Authorization header carries the credential of the client. In MPP, the client sends the payment proof in this header.

terms.plain: The MPP response header that proves a payment settled. It holds a base64url object with `status` (always `success`), `method`, `timestamp` and a method-specific `reference`, such as a Tempo transaction hash or a Stripe PaymentIntent id. Servers send it only with a 2xx response; x402 uses its own `PAYMENT-RESPONSE` header for the same job.
terms.ste: Payment-Receipt is the MPP header that tells the client about a successful payment. The server sends it only with a successful response.

terms.plain: In MPP, the server's offer to be paid, sent in `WWW-Authenticate: Payment`. It names the payment `method`, the `intent`, an encoded `request` with amount and currency, an optional `expires` time and an `id` that the server binds to all of those values, for example with an HMAC. A challenge is single use: a reused or unknown `id` fails with `invalid-challenge`.
terms.ste: In MPP, a challenge tells the client the payment method, the amount and the currency. The client can use each challenge one time only.

terms.plain: In MPP, the client's answer to a challenge. It echoes the `challenge` parameters, adds a method-specific `payload` (a signed transaction, a Shared Payment Token, an encrypted card token and so on) and can name the payer in `source`, preferably as a DID. In verifiable credential systems the same word means a signed claim about a subject, which is a different thing.
terms.ste: In MPP, a credential is the reply of the client to a challenge. The credential contains the proof of payment for the payment method.

terms.plain: In MPP, the kind of payment a challenge asks for, given in the `intent` parameter. The drafts define `charge` (one payment), `session` (metered payments over a channel, Tempo only) and `subscription` (recurring payments). It has nothing to do with a Stripe PaymentIntent object or with Mastercard's Verifiable Intent.
terms.ste: In MPP, the intent tells the type of payment. The three intents are charge, session and subscription.

terms.plain: The MPP intent for a single payment of a fixed `amount` in a given `currency`. The client pays through the named method and retries with a credential, and the server verifies and settles before it sends any part of the response. Every MPP payment method defines a charge.
terms.ste: Charge is the MPP intent for one payment of a fixed amount. The server must verify the payment before it sends the resource.

terms.plain: The MPP intent for metered use, such as paying per model token. The client deposits into an on-chain escrow channel, then sends signed vouchers with a rising `cumulativeAmount` as it consumes the service, and the server settles on-chain when it chooses. The session draft is experimental and defined for the Tempo method in `mpp-specs`.
terms.ste: Session is the MPP intent for a payment that increases with use. The client sends signed vouchers while it uses the service.

terms.plain: The MPP intent for a recurring payment of a fixed `amount` every `periodCount` `periodUnit` (day, week or month). The server collects the first period on activation, returns a `subscriptionId` in the receipt and may collect one renewal per period. Missed periods never add up to extra charges.
terms.ste: Subscription is the MPP intent for a payment that occurs one time in each period. The server can collect only one payment in each period.

terms.plain: A signed off-chain message that raises the total a payee may claim from a payment channel. MPP Tempo sessions send vouchers with a rising `cumulativeAmount`, and the x402 `batch-settlement` scheme uses vouchers with `maxClaimableAmount`. Vouchers cost no fees, and only the latest one matters when the channel settles.
terms.ste: A voucher is a signed message that increases the total amount that the payee can claim. The client sends vouchers off the chain, so they cost no fee.

terms.plain: An on-chain deposit that lets two parties exchange many off-chain payments and settle only the net result. The payer locks funds, sends vouchers as it uses the service, and either side closes the channel; a forced close starts a grace period before the payer can withdraw. MPP Tempo sessions and the x402 `batch-settlement` scheme on EVM both use channels.
terms.ste: A payment channel is a deposit on the chain for many small payments. The two parties settle only the final total on the chain.

terms.plain: The token standard of the Tempo blockchain, built for stablecoins. TIP-20 tokens use 6 decimals, can carry a transfer memo, and can point to a TIP-403 policy registry for allow and block lists. MPP's `tempo` method names the token by its TIP-20 address in `currency`.
terms.ste: TIP-20 is the token standard of the Tempo blockchain. TIP-20 tokens have 6 decimals and can have a memo with each transfer.

terms.plain: A payments blockchain from Tempo Labs, whose team wrote MPP together with Stripe. It has no native gas token: fees are paid in USD TIP-20 stablecoins. Its mainnet chain id is 4217, blocks arrive about every 600 ms, and Simplex BFT consensus gives deterministic finality.
terms.ste: Tempo is a blockchain for payments. On Tempo, the fees are in stablecoins, and the chain has deterministic finality.

terms.plain: An IETF format for machine-readable HTTP error bodies, served as `application/problem+json` with fields such as `type`, `title`, `status` and `detail`. MPP uses it for its error types under `https://paymentauth.org/problems/`, for example `payment-expired`, `invalid-challenge` and `verification-failed`. RFC 9457 replaced RFC 7807 in 2023.
terms.ste: Problem details is an IETF format for HTTP error messages in JSON. MPP uses this format to tell the client why a payment failed.

terms.plain: A hash of an HTTP message body, sent in the `Content-Digest` header defined by RFC 9530. MPP challenges can carry a `digest` parameter so a payment is bound to one exact request body, which matters for POST requests. RFC 9421 signatures can cover the digest header to protect the body, but Visa TAP does not require it, so TAP signatures leave the body unbound.
terms.ste: A content digest is a hash of the body of an HTTP message. MPP uses the digest to connect a payment to one request body.
